title: Workflow-writing skill
description: Installs the writing-github-workflows Agent Skill under .agents/skills: how to write, review and simplify GitHub Actions workflows that read at a glance, with a workflow per trigger, a job per check, one command per step, one naming grammar in which workflows are nouns, jobs verbs and steps sentences, no comment doing a name's job, immutable pins, least privilege, actionlint and zizmor runs, and rewrites of workflows before and after.

content: description: Writes, reviews and simplifies GitHub Actions workflows so each reads at a glance, with a workflow per trigger, a job per check, one command per step, one naming grammar, and no comment doing a name's job. Covers names, triggers, permissions, action pins and lockfiles, timeouts, concurrency, toolchain setup and caches, required checks, and linting with actionlint and zizmor. Use when creating, editing or reviewing anything under .github/workflows, adding CI, a release or a deployment on GitHub, when a workflow grows inline scripts, drift checks or explanatory comments, or when a required check never reports. Not for GitLab CI or other CI systems, nor for the code of a JavaScript or Docker action.

A workflow is read far more often than it is written: by whoever reviews the change, by the developer whose check went red, and by branch protection, which treats job names as an API. Write it as an index of what CI does, not as a program. Every line is a trigger, a privilege, a toolchain, or a command a developer also runs on their own machine. **Logic lives in the project; the workflow wires it to GitHub.**

- **Read what exists**: every file in `.github/workflows/`, the project's entry points (Makefile, mise tasks, `package.json` scripts, justfile, nox or tox sessions, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`) and its pins (`mise.toml`, `.python-version`, `uv.lock`, `packageManager`). A step calls one of those entry points and never re-implements one.
- **Keep the repository's conventions**: how it pins actions (`.github/workflows/actions.lock`, SHA pins, Dependabot or Renovate), `.yml` or `.yaml`, and how it names steps.
- **Find the required checks before renaming a job.** A job's `name`, or its id when it has none, is the name a branch rule requires; `references/naming.md` has the command that lists them.
- **Size the job.** A workflow with one check needs four steps, not a framework. A matrix, a composite action or a reusable workflow earns its place with its second or third caller.

1. **Security beats readability.** Immutable pins, least privilege, untrusted input kept out of scripts and the choice of trigger are never traded for a shorter file. Win readability back through structure: fewer actions, a lockfile instead of SHA pins, a task instead of a script.
2. **A required check's name beats the naming grammar.** Rename a required job only in the same change as the rule that requires it.

3. **The repository's conventions beat this skill's style defaults**, such as case, the file extension and which steps get names. Consistency inside one repository is worth more than agreement with a guide. Rule 1 is not style.
4. **Plain beats DRY.** Two short, similar jobs beat a YAML anchor, a one-entry matrix or a reusable workflow with one caller.
| Unit | Is | Split when | Never split to |

| Workflow | a trigger with a purpose: checks on pull requests, a release, a deployment, a schedule | the trigger or the audience differs | group by tool: a new pull request check is a job in the existing workflow |

| Job | a check someone reads, or work that needs its own runner, permissions, secrets or environment | it must run in parallel, report separately or hold other privileges | label phases: every job pays for a runner, a checkout and a toolchain |
| Step | one command whose failure means one thing | the failures mean different things to the reader | show progress: group long output with `::group::` |
A check job is three to five steps: check out, set up the toolchain, install when the run command does not, run the check. Past six, write down what each step buys and cut the ones that buy nothing.
Workflows are nouns, jobs are verbs, steps are sentences. One grammar lets a reader predict a name before seeing it.
| File | the workflow's name in kebab-case, `.yml` | `ci.yml`, `release.yml`, `docs-site.yml` | `SQL_Format.yaml`, `workflow2.yml` |
| Workflow `name` | short noun phrase, sentence case, no emoji | `CI`, `Release`, `Deployment`, `Docs site`, `Nightly` | `Run CI`, `SQL Format Check Workflow`, `🚀 Deploy` |

| Job id | kebab-case verb, with an object when siblings need one: what the job does, never the tool that does it | `lint`, `test`, `build`, `check-format`, `deploy-staging` | `sqlfmt`, `ruff`, `job1`, `Build_Docs` |
| Job `name` | omitted, so the id is the check's name; set only to word a matrix or keep a name a rule already requires | `Test (${{ matrix.python }})` | `name: sqlfmt` repeating the id |

| Step `name` | imperative in sentence case: a verb, then what the step proves or produces; no full stop | `Check SQL formatting`, `Install dependencies`, `Run unit tests`, `Publish to PyPI` | `Run sqlfmt --diff`, `SQL formatting`, `Checkout code`, `Setup Node` |
| Step `id` | only when something reads it: a kebab-case noun for its output | `version`, `pnpm-store` | an id on every step |

- **Name every `run:` step. Name a `uses:` step only when the action's name hides what it does here**: `actions/checkout` and `setup-*` steps go unnamed; an `actions/upload-artifact` step is `Upload test reports`.

- **One verb per meaning**: `Check` for a read-only check that fails instead of fixing, `Lint`, `Run` for tests, `Set up` for a toolchain (two words; "setup" is the noun), `Install` for dependencies, `Build`, `Publish` to a registry, `Deploy` to an environment, `Upload` and `Download` for artifacts. Never `Ensure`, `Verify that` or `Make sure`.
- **Name the outcome, not the mechanism.** The command already shows the mechanism, so a name that repeats it says nothing.
- **A job is named for its check, not its tool**, so the check, and the rule that requires it, survive a change of tool.
Read `references/naming.md` for where each name appears, rewrites of names that went wrong, matrices, reusable workflows, and keeping required checks intact.

- **A step runs one command a developer could paste into a terminal**, usually one line calling the project's entry point: `uv run pytest`, `pnpm test`, `mise run lint`, `make check`, `./gradlew build`. When CI needs a command no developer runs, decide which side should change.

- **No programs in YAML.** A `run:` block holds at most a few plain commands in sequence: no conditionals or loops, no heredoc in another language, no `python -c`, no parsing another command's output. Logic like that becomes a task in the project's runner or a script file that also runs locally, called in one line, or it is designed away.

- **Delete a drift check by deleting the drift.** A step that checks two files agree, such as a version pinned in two places or a list kept twice, guards a duplication. Make one file the source and derive or delete the other. When a generated copy must stay, check it with its own generator, `<regenerate> && git diff --exit-code`. Never parse YAML or TOML in a step.

- **Configuration belongs to the tool, not the command line.** Paths, excludes, line length and dialect go in the tool's own configuration where it has a key for them, so CI and a developer run the same command. No input or flag that restates a default or does nothing in CI, such as setup-uv's `version: latest` or sqlfmt's `--no-progressbar`, which it already applies without a terminal.

- **No version numbers in the workflow**, except in a matrix that tests several. The project pins its tools and languages (`mise.toml`, `.python-version`, `uv.lock`, `required-version`, `packageManager`) and the setup step reads the pins.

- **One setup step per toolchain, and none for a tool another one provides.** `jdx/mise-action` installs everything `mise.toml` pins. `astral-sh/setup-uv` is enough for a uv project, because uv installs the Python the project pins; `actions/setup-python` beside it is a second source of truth. Use the setup action's own cache before writing an `actions/cache` step.
- **Don't install what the run command installs.** `uv run` syncs the environment it needs, so a `uv sync` step followed by `uv run --no-sync` is two steps doing one job.

- **When order matters, the order is visible.** Put steps in the order the reader should fix them, so the names explain it. When the order protects something beyond CI, it belongs where developers get it too, such as hook order in `.pre-commit-config.yaml` or a make prerequisite.
- **No diagnostic steps**: printing versions, `ls`, `env`, "check that X is installed", `set -x`, `sleep`. A setup action fails loudly, and the log already shows versions.

- **Let the tool explain its failure.** Prefer the tool's own diff, annotations or problem matcher (`--diff`, `--show-diff-on-failure`, the matchers `setup-*` actions register) to a script that prints advice.
Read `references/examples.md` for whole workflows before and after, including one that went from seven steps and an embedded Python program to four steps.

**A comment that explains what a step does means the step is misnamed or does too much: rename or restructure it, then delete the comment.** No header narrating the workflow and no history ("added because…"): the name and trigger say what the workflow is, and the commit says why it changed.
Two kinds stay, one line each:
- the exact version after a SHA pin: `uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1`;
- the reason a line must stay as it is, where a careful reader would otherwise change it and no name can carry the reason.
# One deploy at a time, and never one cancelled halfway.
After, because a group given as a string lets one run at a time and `cancel-in-progress` is false by default:
runs-on: ubuntu-latest # pnpm check drives Chrome, which the arm images lack

- **Checks run on `pull_request`.** Add `push` to the default branch only when something needs that run, such as a status badge, caches that pull requests restore, or a deployment. Add `workflow_dispatch` to anything a person may need to rerun.

- **Never let a filter skip a required workflow.** A workflow skipped by `paths` or `branches` leaves its checks pending, and the pull request cannot merge. Skip inside it with a job-level `if:`, which reports success.
- **`pull_request_target`, `workflow_run` and `issue_comment` run with secrets and write access.** Use one only for a stated reason, and never run the pull request's code under it.
- **`permissions: contents: read` at the top of every workflow.** A job that needs more lists its whole set, because a job's `permissions` replaces the workflow's.

- **Pin every action to something immutable**, through the repository's mechanism: exact tags such as `@v7.0.1` recorded in `.github/workflows/actions.lock`, or a full commit SHA with its version as a comment. A floating tag such as `@v7` is not a pin, and some actions no longer publish one: `astral-sh/setup-uv` has had none since v8.0.0. Pins nobody updates go stale, so where neither Dependabot nor Renovate watches the actions, say so and offer the configuration in `references/security.md`; don't add it unasked.
- **`persist-credentials: false` on every checkout** unless a later step pushes with git.

- **Untrusted input reaches a script only through `env:`**, quoted: `env: TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}` with `run: echo "$TITLE"`. Never put `${{ }}` inside `run:` for anything a contributor controls.
- **`timeout-minutes` on every job**, a few times its usual duration. The default is six hours.

- **Pull request workflows cancel superseded runs**: `group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}` with `cancel-in-progress: true`. A deployment never cancels one in progress: `concurrency: deploy`.
- `runs-on` takes a label, not a one-item list.

Read `references/security.md` when choosing or changing a pinning mechanism, granting a write permission, handling secrets, OIDC or environments, or using a privileged trigger, a cache in a release, or a self-hosted runner. Read `references/toolchains.md` when setting up Python, Node, Java or mise, or caching dependencies.
- A **matrix** for variations of one job.

- A **composite action** in the repository for a run of steps repeated in three or more jobs, referenced as `uses: $/.github/actions/<name>`, which needs no checkout and needs runners at 2.336.0 or later.
- A **reusable workflow** for whole jobs shared between workflows.
- **Avoid YAML anchors.** GitHub has accepted them since September 2025, but without merge keys they save little, and the reader has to jump around the file to read one job.
- Repeat two or three lines before abstracting them.
These are commands for you to run, not lines for a workflow or for a page written for people:
mise x actionlint@1.7.12 shellcheck@0.11.0 -- actionlint   # syntax, expressions, runner labels, shellcheck on run: blocks
uvx zizmor@1.31.1 .github/workflows                          # security audits at the default persona
- Use the repository's own pins of these tools when it has them, and check for newer releases before pinning new ones.
- actionlint 1.7.12 rejects `$/` references; ignore that one error until a release accepts them.
- A self-hosted runner's label needs `.github/actionlint.yaml` with `self-hosted-runner: {labels: [<label>]}`.
- Run each step's command from a clean checkout where you can. A workflow that lints clean but whose command fails is not done.
1. Read it top to bottom and write down, for each step, what it proves or produces. A step with nothing to write down goes.

2. Report findings ranked: unsafe or broken first (floating pins, untrusted input in scripts, privileged triggers, write permissions at the top, actions on a removed runtime), then structure, then names and comments.
3. Give each finding its line, the problem, the fix, and where a removed responsibility now lives, such as "the version check is gone because the hook now runs the locked sqlfmt".
4. Show the whole rewritten file, then the changes outside it that the rewrite depends on.
5. A workflow that already meets the bar gets "no changes needed". Never invent findings to fill a review.
- Every step sets up a toolchain or runs one command a developer can run; no inline program, drift check or diagnostic step is left.
- No comment says what a step does.
- Names follow the grammar, or the repository's own grammar throughout, and no required check was renamed by accident.
- Every action is pinned to a SHA or a locked exact tag, `permissions` is explicit, untrusted input reaches scripts only through `env:`, and every job has `timeout-minutes`.
- No tool or language version appears in the YAML outside a matrix.
- actionlint and zizmor ran on the changed files, and their findings are fixed or reported.
Checked 2026-10-23. GitHub changes Actions every month; recheck versions, and anything in preview, before relying on them.

- GitHub Docs: workflow syntax, the secure use reference, workflow dependency lockfiles, troubleshooting required status checks, reusing workflow configurations. GitHub changelog: 2025-08-15 (SHA-pinning policy), 2025-09-18 (YAML anchors), 2026-07-30 (self-repository references), 2026-09-23 (Node 20 removed), 2026-10-14 (workflow lockfiles, public preview).
- zizmor 1.31.1 audit documentation; actionlint 1.7.12 checks documentation; OpenSSF Scorecard checks.
- uv's GitHub Actions guide and the `astral-sh/setup-uv` v8.0.0 release notes; the pre-commit 4.4.0 changelog (`language: unsupported`); the sqlfmt configuration reference.

- Bitwarden's workflow conventions and `bitwarden/workflow-linter`; the CI workflows of fifteen widely used repositories, among them `astral-sh/uv`, `python/cpython`, `cli/cli`, `pypa/pip` and `dbt-labs/dbt-core`; Pact's CI guide for contributors; Ian Duncan, "GitHub Actions Is Slowly Killing Your Engineering Team" (2026-02-05).

"notes": "Score the workflow a reviewer and a developer whose check failed would read, not the amount of advice. A result fails outright if it leaves an inline program or a drift check in a step, keeps a floating action reference such as @v7 or @main, puts a contributor-controlled ${{ }} expression inside run:, or renames a job without saying that a required check may depend on its name. A review fails if it invents findings for a workflow that already meets the bar or restructures one the user asked only to change in one place. Removing a check without saying where its responsibility went is a failure even when the check was redundant. In the co-loaded case, the commit message or pull request description follows its own skill and carries no lint output.",

"prompt": "You made this too complicated. Simplify it.

```yaml
---
name: SQL Format

# sqlfmt needs no Snowflake login, so this check runs apart from the
# pre-commit job in pr-checks.yml, which needs one for SQLFluff.
on:
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main
      - develop

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  sqlfmt:
    name: sqlfmt
    runs-on: ["atmos-aws-arc-runner-set"]
    timeout-minutes: 10

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: '3.11'

      - name: Install uv
        uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v4
        with:
          version: "latest"

      - name: Install the dev tools
        run: uv sync --frozen --only-group dev

      - name: Check that the sqlfmt hook pins the locked versions
        run: |
          uv run --no-sync python - <<'EOF'
          import importlib.metadata
          import sys

          import yaml

          with open(".pre-commit-config.yaml") as f:
              repos = yaml.safe_load(f)["repos"]
          hook = next(r for r in repos if r["repo"] == "https://github.com/tconbeer/sqlfmt")
          rev = "v" + importlib.metadata.version("shandy-sqlfmt")
          black = "black==" + importlib.metadata.version("black")
          if hook["rev"] != rev or black not in hook["hooks"][0].get("additional_dependencies", []):
              sys.exit(
                  f"The sqlfmt hook in .pre-commit-config.yaml must pin rev {rev} and {black}, as uv.lock does. "
                  "Bump both together, then run `make fmt` and commit the result."
              )
          EOF

      # Before sqlfmt: its diff would show a bare camelCase key lowercased, and
      # applying that diff makes the column NULL.
      - name: Check that semi-structured keys are quoted
        run: uv run --no-sync pre-commit run quote-json-keys --all-files

      - name: Check SQL formatting
        run: uv run --no-sync sqlfmt --diff --no-progressbar models tests snapshots analyses
```",
"expected_output": "A rewrite of four or five steps with no inline program, the version check replaced by one source of truth for the sqlfmt and black versions, and a list of what moved where.",
"The Python heredoc is gone and no other inline program, conditional or loop replaces it",
"It explains that the version check guarded two copies of the same pins, and removes one copy, showing the change to .pre-commit-config.yaml or to the dependency group that this needs",
"actions/setup-python and the hard-coded 3.11 are gone, and no Python version appears in the workflow",
"There is no separate uv sync step and no --no-sync flag",
"setup-uv is pinned to an exact release, by SHA with a version comment or as an exact tag recorded in a lockfile, and version: latest is gone",
"Every action reference is a full SHA with a version comment or an exact tag in a lockfile; none is a floating tag such as @v7",
"No comment in the result explains what a step does",
"Step names are sentence-case imperatives, checkout and setup steps carry no name, and no name repeats its command",
"The job id names the check rather than the tool, and no job name repeats the id",
"It proposes making the check a job of the existing pull request workflow, or gives a concrete reason to keep a separate workflow",
"It warns that renaming the sqlfmt job changes the check name a branch rule may require",
"--no-progressbar is gone, and permissions and timeout-minutes remain"

"Every run: step is one line, runs uv run with the project's own tools, and has a sentence-case imperative name",
"permissions: contents: read is set, every job has timeout-minutes, and concurrency cancels superseded pull request runs",

"It adds no file beyond the workflow unasked; a Dependabot configuration for the new pins is offered, not created"

"prompt": "Review our CI workflow before I merge it.

    branches: [main]

  contents: read

```",

The SHAs below are the commits of the releases in their comments on 2026-10-23. Resolve current ones before copying: `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/commits/<tag> --jq .sha`.
- A pull request workflow from scratch
- A check that grew a program
- A release that compared the tag with the version
- A deployment whose logic belonged to its task
## A pull request workflow from scratch

A uv project with ruff and pytest. `push` to `main` is there because setup-uv's cache, saved on `main`, is what pull requests restore. `UV_LOCKED` makes every `uv run` fail on a stale `uv.lock`, so the commands stay the ones developers type.
No Python version appears: uv installs the one `.python-version` pins. No `uv sync` step: `uv run` installs what it runs.
## A check that grew a program
Before: seven steps, a Python program in a heredoc, and two comments explaining the YAML.
# sqlfmt needs no Snowflake login, so this check runs apart from the

| Name | Shown in | Breaks when changed |
| File path | the workflow's identity: badge URLs, `gh workflow run <file>`, and the Actions sidebar when `name` is missing | badges, scripts and documents that link it |
| Workflow `name` | the Actions sidebar, the first half of each check in a pull request, the badge's text | nothing matches on it |
| `run-name` | each run in the list of runs; by default the commit message or pull request title | nothing |
| Job id, or job `name` when set | the check's name on pull requests and commits, with matrix values appended; what branch rules require | required checks; `needs:` and `needs.<id>` read the id |
| Step `name` | the job's log; a step without one shows `Run` and its command's first line, or `Run owner/repo@<ref>`, which is a 40-character SHA once pinned | nothing |
| Step `id` | expressions such as `steps.<id>.outputs.<name>` | every expression that reads it |

A pull request lists each check as `<workflow name> / <job name> (<event>)`, such as `CI / test (pull_request)`. A required check matches the job's name with its matrix suffix and ignores the workflow's name, so two workflows with a job called `test` make one ambiguous check: keep job names unique across every workflow in the repository.

An id starts with a letter or `_` and holds letters, digits, `-` and `_`. Hyphens work in expressions, as in `needs.check-format.result`. An expression that names a missing id evaluates to an empty string without an error, which is one more reason to add ids only where something reads them.

- **Workflows are nouns**, because the sidebar lists what the repository has: `CI`, `Release`, `Deployment`, `Nightly`. `CI` is the usual name for the workflow that checks pull requests; nine of fifteen widely used repositories sampled in October 2026 use exactly that.

- **Files mirror the name** in kebab-case with `.yml`, so the file behind a sidebar entry is predictable: `CI` is `ci.yml`, `Docs site` is `docs-site.yml`. A workflow that only other workflows call takes a `reusable-` prefix, `reusable-build.yml`, so nobody looks for its trigger. Renaming a file breaks badges and `gh workflow run` calls, so rename deliberately.

- **Jobs are verbs**, because a check reads as what CI did: `CI / lint`, `CI / test`, `CI / check-format`, `Deployment / deploy-production`. Name the activity, never the tool: `typecheck`, not `mypy`; `check-format`, not `sqlfmt`. Tools are replaced more often than the checks they run, and a rule requires the check's name.

- **Steps are imperative sentences**, verb first and in sentence case, because the log reads as a list of instructions carried out: `Install dependencies`, `Check SQL formatting`, `Publish to PyPI`. Thirteen of the fifteen repositories put the verb first.
- **Ids are nouns for what they hold**: `version`, `pnpm-store`, `wheel-path`.
| `Set up` | a toolchain; usually unnamed, since the action says it | `Set up Python` |
| `Check` | a read-only check that fails instead of fixing | `Check SQL formatting`, `Check types`, `Check links` |
| `Log in to` | a registry or cloud | `Log in to GHCR` |
`Set up` and `Log in` are verbs; `setup` and `login` are nouns. Never `Ensure`, `Verify that`, `Make sure`, `Handle` or `Process`: they say that something happens, not what.

| `sql-format.yml` named `SQL Format`, one job, triggered like the pull request workflow | a `check-format` job in the existing pull request workflow | a check on the same trigger is a job, not a workflow |
| job `sqlfmt` with `name: sqlfmt` | job `check-format`, no `name` | named for its check; the `name` repeated the id |
| `name: Checkout code` on `actions/checkout` | no name | the action says it, and "checkout" is the noun |
| `name: Setup Node.js` on `actions/setup-node` | no name; `Set up Node.js` where the repository names every step | as above |
| `name: Install the dev tools` running `uv sync` | gone | `uv run` installs what it runs |
| `name: Check that the sqlfmt hook pins the locked versions` | gone | the duplication it guarded was removed |
| `name: Check that semi-structured keys are quoted` | `Check semi-structured keys are quoted` | "that" adds nothing |

- GitHub appends a matrix job's values to its name, as in `test (3.12, ubuntu-latest)`. Leave `name` off unless the wording matters. A `name` that contains any matrix expression gets nothing appended, so it must use every matrix variable, or two jobs end up with the same name.
- Changing a matrix value, or the order of its keys, changes the check names, and with them the required checks.
- A job that calls a reusable workflow shows as `<calling job> / <called job>`. Name the calling job for what it does, as you would any job.

- A workflow skipped by a `paths` or `branches` filter leaves its checks pending; a job skipped by `if:` reports success. So decide inside the workflow, with job-level `if:`.

Checked 2026-10-23. Lockfiles and the `pull_request_target` policy were moving that month; recheck both before relying on them.

A tag can move. In March 2025 an attacker repointed the tags of `tj-actions/changed-files` at a commit that printed secrets into build logs, and through `reviewdog/action-setup@v1`, called by other actions, the same campaign reached workflows whatever their own pins said. Pin every action to something that cannot move.
| Mechanism | In the YAML | Covers | State on 2026-10-23 |

| Workflow lockfile, `.github/workflows/actions.lock` | exact tags: `actions/checkout@v7.0.1` | each action and the actions it calls; not reusable workflows from other repositories, nor container images | public preview since 2026-10-14, github.com only; zizmor and OpenSSF Scorecard do not read it yet |
| SHA pin | `actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1` | the action named, not what it calls | what zizmor, Scorecard and GitHub's SHA-pinning policy check |
Use the one the repository uses. A repository with neither gets SHA pins: every plan and every linter understands them. The lockfile is the readable choice once a team accepts a preview.
Never pin a branch (`@main`) or a floating major tag (`@v7`). An action without a major tag, such as `astral-sh/setup-uv` since v8.0.0, is a reminder that the tag was never a pin.
gh api repos/actions/checkout/releases/latest --jq .tag_name   # the newest release
gh api repos/actions/checkout/commits/v7.0.1 --jq .sha         # the commit it points at
The comment carries the full version, `# v7.0.1`, never `# v7`: zizmor's `ref-version-mismatch` audit compares the two, and Dependabot rewrites the comment with the SHA.
gh actions-lock            # write or fix the lockfile, narrowing @v7 to the exact tag
gh actions-lock --verify   # check without writing, as in CI
Rerun `gh actions-lock` after every change to a `uses:`. A same-repository `./` action that calls remote actions has to become `$/` first, which `--migrate-local-actions` does.

Dependabot moves the SHA and its comment together, and regenerates a lockfile entry in the same pull request. It waits three days after a release by default; zizmor's `dependabot-cooldown` audit asks for seven. It raises no security alerts for SHA-pinned actions, so zizmor's online `known-vulnerable-actions` audit is what catches a vulnerable pin. Renovate pins and updates SHAs with the `helpers:pinGitHubActionDigests` preset.
- `permissions: contents: read` at the top of the workflow. Every scope a `permissions` block does not list is `none`.
- A job's `permissions` replaces the workflow's, so a job that needs more lists its whole set, `contents: read` included.

- The usual grants, each on the one job that needs it: `id-token: write` for OIDC, such as trusted publishing or a cloud login; `packages: write` to push to GHCR; `contents: write` to push tags or create releases; `pull-requests: write` to comment; `pages: write` with `id-token: write` to deploy Pages; `security-events: write` to upload SARIF.

- `persist-credentials: false` on `actions/checkout` unless a later step pushes with git. Since checkout v6 the persisted token sits outside the workspace, but every later step in the job can still read it.

A contributor controls the pull request's title, body and branch name (`github.head_ref`), commit messages, issue, comment and review bodies, and most of `github.event`. `${{ }}` is expanded into the script before the shell sees it, so any of these inside `run:` is code injection. Pass them through `env:` and quote the variable; `${{ env.NAME }}` inside `run:` is templated too, so write `"$NAME"`.
Variables the runner sets, such as `GITHUB_REF_NAME` and `GITHUB_SHA`, are already in the environment; read them as `"$GITHUB_REF_NAME"` instead of through `${{ github.ref_name }}`.
- `pull_request` from a fork runs with a read-only token and no secrets. It is the trigger for checks.

- `pull_request_target`, `workflow_run` and `issue_comment` run in the base repository with its secrets and, often, write access. Code from the pull request is data there: never built, installed or run. Since v7, `actions/checkout` refuses a fork's code under `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run` unless given `allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true`; needing that input is the sign to stop.
- For privilege separation, the unprivileged `pull_request` workflow uploads its results and a `workflow_run` workflow reads them as data.

- Public repositories have a default policy that blocks `pull_request_target`. It runs in evaluate mode now; GitHub's page on securely using `pull_request_target` gives 2026-12-02 as the date it is enforced.
- Give a secret to the step that needs it, through that step's `env:`, never to the whole workflow.
- Prefer OIDC to stored keys: PyPI trusted publishing (`uv publish` uses it on GitHub Actions with no token, once the PyPI project trusts the workflow), and cloud logins that assume a role.
- Put deployment secrets in an `environment:` with required reviewers; the job cannot read them until someone approves.
- Never `secrets: inherit`, `toJSON(secrets)`, or one secret holding a JSON document.

- A cache saved by one run is restored by others, so a release or publish job restores none: `cache-mode: none` on the job, or the setup action's cache turned off. setup-uv already leaves its cache off for tag pushes and releases.
- Since September 2026 `cache-mode` (`read`, `write`, `write-only`, `none`) sets cache access per workflow or job, and low-trust triggers such as `pull_request_target` get `read` by default.
- A self-hosted runner never serves a public repository: a fork's pull request would run on it.
- Prefer ephemeral self-hosted runners, such as Actions Runner Controller or just-in-time runners; a persistent one keeps whatever the last job left.

- `$/` references need runner 2.336.0 or later. Runners run every JavaScript action on Node 24 since 2026-09-23, so an action release that still declares `node20`, such as setup-uv v4, is due for an upgrade.

- **actionlint** types expressions, checks ids, runner labels and action inputs, and runs shellcheck on `run:` blocks when shellcheck is on the `PATH`. Its input checks for popular actions only work on `@vN` references, so SHA-pinned steps lose them. 1.7.12, the release current on 2026-10-23, rejects `$/` references.

- **zizmor** audits security. At the default persona it wants every action hash-pinned (since 1.20), `persist-credentials: false`, no `${{ }}` from untrusted contexts in scripts, least-privilege permissions, no cache in release workflows and trusted publishing where a registry offers it. `--persona=pedantic` also asks for a `name` on every job and for `concurrency` limits; this skill leaves job names off on purpose, so pedantic's `anonymous-definition` findings are expected.
- In CI, `zizmorcore/zizmor-action` runs zizmor; actionlint has a Docker image and pre-commit hooks. Pin both like any other action.

Releases checked 2026-10-23. Before pinning, check for a newer one with `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest --jq .tag_name`, then find the commit it points at with `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/commits/<tag> --jq .sha`.

1. **The repository pins its tools in `mise.toml`**: one `jdx/mise-action` step installs all of them, and `mise run <task>` is the entry point when the project has tasks. Don't add a language's setup action beside it.
2. **Otherwise one setup action per language**, reading the project's own version file, never a version typed into the workflow.

3. **No setup step for a tool another step provides** (Python under uv, Node under `pnpm/setup`), and no action for something the runner already has: zizmor's `superfluous-actions` audit flags such actions, `softprops/action-gh-release` where `gh release create` does the job.
- uv installs the Python that `.python-version` or `requires-python` pins. `actions/setup-python` beside it saves about a second on GitHub-hosted runners and adds a second pin.

- setup-uv installs the uv version that `required-version` in `pyproject.toml` or `uv.toml` asks for, else the newest; `version: latest` changes nothing. It has published no major tags since v8.0.0, so pin the exact release.

- `UV_LOCKED: 1` in the workflow's `env` makes every `uv run` fail on a stale `uv.lock`, which keeps each command the one developers type; `--locked` does the same for one command. `--frozen` skips the check and hides a forgotten `uv lock`.
- `uv run --only-group <group>` installs that dependency group without the project, for a job that needs the dev tools only.
- Don't set `activate-environment`; setup-uv's documentation recommends `uv run` instead.
- setup-uv's cache is on by default on GitHub-hosted runners, and off on self-hosted runners and for tag pushes, releases, `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run`.
With pnpm 11 or later, `pnpm/setup` is the whole setup: it installs the pnpm that `packageManager` names, the runtime that `devEngines.runtime` or `.nvmrc` names, and then runs `pnpm install`.
With pnpm 10 or earlier, `pnpm/action-setup` (which reads `packageManager`) comes before `actions/setup-node` with `node-version-file` and `cache: pnpm`, then a `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` step.
`setup-gradle` caches Gradle's state, so the job needs no `actions/cache`. When `mise.toml` pins the JDK, `jdx/mise-action` replaces `setup-java`.
- It installs every tool `mise.toml` pins, `--locked` against `mise.lock` when there is one, and caches them by default. `install_args: node` limits a job to the tools it needs.
- mise can pin uv and Python as well, so a uv project whose tools live in `mise.toml` needs no setup-uv.
- A release job sets `cache: false`, because mise trusts a restored tool cache as it is.
- Use the setup action's own cache: setup-uv's `enable-cache`, `pnpm/setup`'s `cache`, setup-node's `cache`, setup-java's `cache` or `setup-gradle`, mise-action's `cache`.
- Write an `actions/cache` step only for what no setup action caches, keyed on the lockfile: `key: <tool>-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('<lockfile>') }}`.
- Release and publish jobs restore no cache, because a cache saved by one run is restored by others: `cache-mode: none` on the job, or the setup action's cache turned off.
